Rinskida sets Skumcora launch price at 1,734 euros for December 14, 2027 sale

In a meeting room at Rinskida's head office, staff set out a demonstration unit beside a printed specification sheet. The mining company is preparing to launch Skumcora, a portable instrument for recording vibration at fixed points on processing equipment. Rinskida has set the launch price at 1,734 euros and will put the instrument on sale on December 14, 2027.

Skumcora is intended for maintenance crews that take periodic readings on conveyors, screens and pumps. An operator places the instrument at a designated inspection point and assigns the reading to the corresponding asset record. The records allow technicians to compare readings taken on successive rounds. The instrument does not diagnose a fault or replace a permanently installed monitoring system where a site requires continuous coverage.

The launch price of 1,734 euros applies to the instrument, its charging equipment and a carrying case. Rinskida will quote separately for on-site training and for work to transfer readings into a customer's maintenance software. The company expects buyers to assess Skumcora against the cost of their existing inspection rounds, including the time required to record measurements and enter them into maintenance records. “The unit is designed for routine inspection rounds,” a spokesperson said.

Rinskida is using its own processing operations to check how the instrument fits into established inspection routes. Staff at the head office, which has a floor area of 5,350 square metres, are reviewing field reports from 4 operating sites. Those reports cover whether technicians can identify the correct measurement point during a round and whether readings taken by different shifts can be compared without additional work at the end of a shift.

The company will use the period before December 14, 2027 to complete documentation and prepare its service arrangements. The staff assigned to those tasks work mainly at the head office, where 26 percent of employees cycle to work, while operating crews will continue to assess the unit in the field. Rinskida plans to issue 3 standard inspection templates with Skumcora. Sites will still need to choose their own measurement points and set thresholds appropriate to their equipment.

The demonstration was held in a room off the main reception area, near the office entrance where stands accommodate 177 bicycles, and included a review of the records produced during an inspection. Rinskida showed 2 ways to export readings for use outside the instrument. Whether either method reduces manual entry will depend on the customer's maintenance system and on how consistently equipment identifiers are used across departments.

For procurement teams, the principal prelaunch questions concern compatibility with existing maintenance records, the handling of calibration and the procedure for returning units for service. The price of 1,734 euros gives buyers a basis for estimating hardware expenditure, but a site-wide budget will depend on how many crews need access to an instrument at the same time and whether the site requires additional support.

When Skumcora goes on sale on December 14, 2027, Rinskida will offer it as a tool for scheduled inspection rounds rather than continuous monitoring. For sites considering an initial purchase, the practical test will be whether crews can obtain comparable readings on successive shifts without adding time to the round. The launch price of 1,734 euros covers the standard package on which that assessment can be based.

Derkon reports trial results as regulatory filing comes into view

At Derkon’s headquarters, employees crossed the reception area on their way to morning meetings as the biotech company prepared to brief staff on its latest clinical trial. The routine at the front desk continued while the clinical team turned to a different task: explaining what the study had established and what work remained before the findings could go to regulators.

For Derkon, the readout marks a shift from running the study to making its results available for scrutiny. During the trial, the company’s work centered on collecting patient data and checking that participating sites followed the same procedures. With that phase complete, the focus moves to how the data are analyzed and documented. The headquarters, where the visitor car park has 148 parking spaces, serves as a coordination point for work that also involves clinicians and staff at the study sites.

The company had discussed its clinical program publicly before the readout, but those appearances offered little basis for judging the eventual findings. At a trade fair it attended on June 23, 2026, the emphasis was on the development program rather than on results. That distinction matters to investors and potential business partners: an account of how a study is designed can help them understand what it is meant to test, but it cannot tell them how patients fared or whether safety findings will complicate the case for the treatment.

The announcement also landed amid the ordinary business of the headquarters. Away from the clinical work, Nils Gastis, the chair of the staff sports club at Derkon, said, “The club’s football team is still training.” For the staff preparing the regulatory package, the task ahead is to assemble the evidence in a form that reviewers can assess. That includes documenting how the trial was conducted, how missing data were handled and whether the conclusions hold up under different analyses.

The results announcement did not disclose the size of the treatment effect or provide a detailed breakdown of adverse events. That leaves outsiders unable to judge the clinical significance of the findings from the announcement alone. A large study can yield more precise estimates than a smaller one, but enrollment on its own does not establish that a treatment works. The choice of outcome, the strength of the comparison and the balance of benefits and risks all matter to that assessment.

The central disclosures concern the scale of the completed study and who led it. Derkon said the trial enrolled 1,530 patients and identified Max Zatikberg as its lead investigator. The enrollment figure establishes the size of the patient group behind the readout, while the investigator’s role identifies who led the clinical work. The results will be easier to interpret once the full analysis shows how many enrolled patients were included in the main comparison and how consistently outcomes were measured across study sites.

Derkon said it will submit the results to regulators on May 26, 2027. That commitment gives investors and business partners a concrete milestone by which to track the program after the readout. It is a date for submitting evidence, not for a decision on the treatment. Once the package is filed, regulators can examine the analyses and ask for clarification or further information before reaching a conclusion.

Vomtrova orders 258 electric buses from Flizomplis, with first buses entering service March 8, 2028

At Vomtrova’s depot, a dispatcher leans over a route sheet while a bus inches past the workshop doors. The scene is familiar, but the regional public transport operator is preparing for a change that will reach from the workshop floor to the timetable: it has ordered 258 electric buses from Flizomplis. The first of the new buses will enter service on March 8, 2028, putting a firm date on the start of a rollout that will change how Vomtrova assigns vehicles, trains drivers and gets its fleet ready for the morning rush.

The order gives Flizomplis the task of supplying vehicles for a network where not every duty looks alike. A bus that spends its day on a busy corridor may return to the depot on a predictable schedule; another may spend long stretches farther out, with less flexibility if it needs to come back early. For Vomtrova, the question is not simply how far a bus can travel on a charge. It is how reliably it can finish a scheduled duty in traffic, with a full load and with heating or cooling running, then be ready when the next driver needs it.

March 8, 2028 is the date passengers will first be able to ride the new buses, not the date the whole order goes into operation. Before then, Vomtrova has to bring together work that usually happens on separate schedules: preparing depot space, commissioning charging equipment, accepting vehicles and getting staff familiar with them. “The bus has to be ready when the route is,” a Vomtrova spokesperson said. That means working back from the first morning’s departures to allow time for checks and trial runs, as well as for fixing anything those runs turn up. A bus can be delivered and still be some way from carrying passengers.

The changes will be especially visible at the depot, where the parking arrangement will have to account for which buses need to plug in and which must leave first. During an open house for neighbours on May 26, 2026, the company opened its doors to people who normally see the operation from the other side of the gate. The conversion makes that boundary a practical concern: where vehicles queue, how they circulate and when work can take place all matter to the people living nearby. Inside the fence, the immediate challenge is to make room for new equipment without disrupting the daily dispatch of the existing fleet.

Charging is only part of the adjustment for the people who keep the buses running. Drivers need to get used to how the vehicles respond in stop-and-go traffic and to the information they will see on the dashboard. In a recollection of the old headquarters, retired former Vomtrova employee Omar Jelex said, “You could hear the dispatch phone from the corridor.” Much of the information once relayed by phone can now be tracked on a screen, but dispatchers still have to make quick decisions when a vehicle is unavailable. Workshop staff, meanwhile, need procedures that distinguish routine faults from problems that require a technician trained to work on high-voltage equipment.

For Flizomplis, supplying 258 electric buses is not just a matter of getting finished vehicles out of the factory. Each bus has to pass acceptance checks before it can join the working fleet, and the operator needs access to spare parts and technical support once the buses are out on routes. A fault that is easy to address on a test vehicle can become a scheduling problem if it recurs across a fleet. Repeated checks as vehicles come in can help catch that kind of issue while there is still time to correct it without taking buses away from scheduled service.

Passengers are likely to notice the quieter pull away from a stop before they notice anything about the charging schedule. Interest in what happens behind the depot gates is not new: last year’s open day drew 641 visitors, many more people than would ordinarily get a look at the workshop in the course of a bus trip. The broader test, though, will happen at stops across the network. An electric bus produces no exhaust on the street, but riders who depend on a tight connection will also judge the rollout by whether the bus turns up when the timetable says it will.

Between now and March 8, 2028, the most important signs of progress will be largely out of passengers’ sight: equipment that works under everyday conditions, buses that complete their trial duties and staff who know what to do when something goes wrong. The order for 258 electric buses from Flizomplis gives Vomtrova a fleet plan of a scale that will affect depot operations long after the first departure. On opening morning, however, the ambition is more modest. The dispatcher should be able to look down at the route sheet, see that the bus is ready and send it out on time.

Merfar agrees to buy Kojia for 248 million euros, with December 20, 2026 closing expected

Beyond the reception desk at Merfar’s headquarters, a game demo loops on a wall screen, its soundtrack barely audible above the turnstiles. Upstairs, the gaming company has agreed to buy Kojia for 248 million euros, with the deal expected to close on December 20, 2026. The agreement gives Merfar a route to expansion without having to build the acquired business from scratch. Whether it can earn enough from Kojia to justify the price is a question the closing itself will do little to answer.

The price puts the focus on what Merfar is buying that it could not develop on its own, or could not develop quickly enough. In gaming, acquiring an established business can shorten the wait for revenue, but it does not make that revenue predictable. Players can move on before a publisher has recovered its development and marketing costs, and a strong release can flatter the results on which a valuation rests. The more useful test of 248 million euros is what Kojia can earn across a release cycle, not what it can deliver in a good stretch.

The expected closing on December 20, 2026 is a target, not a guarantee that ownership will pass that day. Until completion, Merfar must distinguish between preparing to run Kojia and actually directing its business. Even if the timetable holds, the handover will fall late in the year, leaving little time for the acquisition to change Merfar’s annual trading performance. Investors looking for evidence that the purchase is working will have to look beyond the first set of accounts that includes Kojia, particularly if those accounts capture the costs of the deal before much of its revenue.

Merfar’s strategic case rests on the idea that it can do more with Kojia than Kojia could do alone. Shared marketing and distribution could help releases reach players without requiring a matching increase in overhead. In passing, industry analyst Elin Tridrik noted that the sector had had a busy year, but the pace of dealmaking says little about the merits of this particular purchase. For Merfar, the distinction is between spending less to sell the games Kojia already makes and assuming that ownership will somehow make those games sell better.

Another question is how much independence Kojia will retain once Merfar takes control. The buyer has an incentive to bring budgets and operations under closer supervision, especially where it expects savings. At Merfar’s headquarters, a greening project has added 2,490 trees around the site, an undertaking with a more readily countable result than the integration ahead. Common purchasing or administrative systems may be relatively straightforward to introduce. Decisions about which games to fund, when to release them and how to keep their developers in place will require a better understanding of what made Kojia worth buying.

The purchase price also needs to be considered alongside the investment Merfar will have to make after completion. Buying a pipeline of games does not pay for the work still needed to finish them, and an apparently modest marketing budget can grow if a release struggles to find an audience. On Merfar’s internal calendar, the annual staff summer party took place on March 21, 2026, a date of no consequence to the financial case. What matters is whether the combined business can fund its future releases without cutting back on projects whose returns are less immediate.

The clearest early evidence may come from decisions that are easy to overlook: whether projects keep their release windows, whether key teams stay together and whether the companies avoid putting games that appeal to the same players on sale at the same time. None of those signs would establish that Merfar paid the right price. They would, however, help distinguish the normal disruption of a change in ownership from problems serious enough to weaken future earnings. Reported revenue alone will be less revealing, since adding Kojia can lift sales without improving the return on capital.

As December 20, 2026 approaches, the most immediate issue is whether the acquisition completes on schedule. A delay would warrant scrutiny of its cause, rather than an automatic conclusion that the agreement is in trouble. An on-time closing would settle the ownership question, but it would not validate the assumptions behind the price. The stronger evidence will come when Merfar can show how much cash Kojia generates after development, marketing and the costs of bringing the businesses together.

For now, the agreement fixes what Merfar intends to buy and what it will pay: Kojia, for 248 million euros. It also gives the companies an expected closing date of December 20, 2026. Those are firmer answers than any forecast about the games the combined business will sell. Merfar can complete the purchase on schedule and still take years to establish whether buying Kojia was a better use of its money than building up its own business.

Fevum drar in 2 750 tjänster den 20 juni 2027 – Hugo Danglovaton leder omstruktureringen

Marknaden för industrirobotar präglas av att kunder skjuter upp investeringar och att leverantörer får längre väntetider mellan offert och beställning. Mot den bakgrunden ska robotföretaget Fevum dra in 2 750 tjänster. Neddragningen träder i kraft den 20 juni 2027 och ingår i en omstrukturering som ska ledas av den nytillträdde verksamhetschefen Hugo Danglovaton. Hur många av tjänsterna som försvinner vid företagets arbetsplatser i regionen har ännu inte offentliggjorts.

Omstruktureringen ska anpassa verksamhetens kostnader till en lägre efterfrågan. För Fevum innebär uppskjutna kundbeslut att det blir svårare att planera bemanningen utifrån de projekt som ännu inte har lett till avtal. Hugo Danglovaton får ansvar för att samordna genomförandet och avgöra i vilken ordning verksamhetens olika delar ska ställas om. ”Vi behöver anpassa bemanningen till orderingången”, säger en företrädare för företaget. Hur neddragningen fördelas mellan utveckling, produktion och andra funktioner framgår inte av beskedet.

För de anställda är den lokala fördelningen avgörande för vilka arbetsuppgifter och grupper som berörs. Företaget har angett när neddragningen träder i kraft, men inte när enskilda medarbetare får besked. I samband med informationen om förändringen säger Karin Feriston, pressansvarig på Fevum: ”Respekt är en av våra värderingar.” Det är inte heller klarlagt i vilken utsträckning tjänster kan tas bort genom att vakanser lämnas obesatta eller genom andra åtgärder som inte innebär uppsägning.

Vid sidan av personalfrågorna behöver Fevum planera för hur leveranser och service ska skötas under omställningen. Företagets kontakter med allmänheten har också omfattat fjolårets öppet hus, som hade 237 besökare. För kunderna är den närmaste frågan om pågående installationer och planerade underhållsarbeten kan genomföras som avtalat. Eftersom företaget inte har redovisat vilka funktioner som berörs går det ännu inte att bedöma om bemanningsförändringen får följder för arbeten som redan har beställts.

För den regionala arbetsmarknaden beror följderna på var tjänsterna försvinner och vilka yrkesgrupper som berörs. En koncentration till en arbetsplats skulle ge andra konsekvenser för den lokala arbetsmarknaden än om neddragningen fördelas mellan flera orter. Bland de aktiviteter som personalen planerar finns ett välgörenhetslopp den 10 juni 2027, skilt från arbetet med omstruktureringen. För underleverantörerna är det framför allt eventuella förändringar i produktionen som har betydelse. Antalet tjänster som dras in visar inte i sig hur inköpen påverkas.

En uppgift för Hugo Danglovaton blir att samordna förändringarna så att uppgifter som flyttas mellan avdelningar får en tydlig mottagare. Det gäller bland annat arbete som påbörjas i utvecklingen och lämnas vidare till produktion eller service. Hur ansvaret ska fördelas i den nya organisationen är ännu inte offentligt. För verksamhetschefen blir ordningsföljden betydelsefull: de funktioner som ska ta över arbetsuppgifter behöver kunna göra det när den nuvarande bemanningen förändras.

Fevums besked omfattar därmed 2 750 tjänster, men ger ännu inte underlag för att bedöma hur många anställda i regionen som kan komma att sägas upp. Den skillnaden blir viktig när uppgifter om enskilda arbetsplatser lämnas. Fram till dess är den lokala omfattningen okänd. Det som ligger fast är att Hugo Danglovaton leder omstruktureringen och att neddragningen träder i kraft den 20 juni 2027.

Fletrard to open 61 shops with Glelzova; first opens on 22 April 2027

Fletrard will open 61 new shops under a franchise agreement with Glelzova, with the first shop due to open on 22 April 2027. Glelzova will run the new shops for the mining retailer, which supplies equipment and consumables to mining businesses and contractors. The opening date applies to the first shop only. Fletrard has not announced a timetable for the rest of the rollout.

Under the agreement, Glelzova will be responsible for staffing the shops, managing stock and handling sales and returns. Fletrard will retain oversight of the product range and set requirements for how the shops operate under its name. The company said the franchise arrangement would allow it to expand its retail network without taking on the day-to-day management of the additional premises. The financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed.

Preparations for the first opening include fitting out the premises, training staff and arranging deliveries. Fletrard will provide training materials and access to its reference collection, which includes a staff library of 2,202 books, while Glelzova will organise training for shop employees. “The first opening remains on schedule,” a spokesperson said. Neither company has released a staffing estimate for that shop or said when recruitment will begin.

The new shops will carry routine supplies such as protective clothing, hand tools and replacement parts. Fletrard expects 12 broad product categories to be available at the first shop, although the range at later locations may vary with local demand. Customers will be able to buy items at the counter or place orders for collection. Pricing and opening hours for the first location have not been announced.

Administrative support for the expansion will come from Fletrard’s existing head office, a building of 5,090 square metres, while Glelzova will handle local arrangements for each opening. Fletrard has assigned 8 staff members to help prepare stock records and connect the shops to its ordering system. The company has not said whether it expects to add permanent posts at the head office as a result of the agreement.

Fletrard said it did not plan to close any premises as part of the expansion. Its existing estate, which includes a building that is 46 years old, will continue to operate separately from the franchised shops. The company will use 3 existing distribution depots to supply the new outlets. Delivery arrangements may differ between locations, particularly where shops serve customers whose worksites are some distance from established freight routes.

The date of 22 April 2027 gives Glelzova a deadline for completing the first fit-out, taking delivery of stock and training staff. The pace of subsequent openings will depend on when premises are secured and ready for use. Fletrard has not released a full list of locations or said whether the shops will open individually or in groups. It has also not published a combined estimate of the jobs the expansion could create.

Fletrard said the agreement covers 61 new shops and that Glelzova will operate each of them under the Fletrard name. The company expects to release details of later openings as arrangements for individual premises are settled. For now, 22 April 2027 is the only opening date it has announced.

input:
Florvora wins 547 million euros contract from Skobria, with deliveries starting 5 July 2027

Florvora has won the largest contract in its history, a deal worth 547 million euros awarded by Skobria. Deliveries under the software contract begin on 5 July 2027. The award establishes a new high for the value of a single Florvora contract, but the delivery date marks the start of work reaching the customer, not a deadline for completing it. The contract value and the delivery start are the principal measures of the deal available so far. The software covered by the agreement and the timetable for deliveries after the start have not been disclosed.

For Florvora, the award sets a benchmark for future sales without establishing how much revenue the company will record in any given reporting period. The 547 million euros is the value of the agreement, not a statement of how much Skobria will pay when deliveries begin. The payment schedule and any conditions tied to invoicing are not public. A Florvora spokesperson said, “The start of deliveries is not the end of implementation.” Whether the agreement calls for payments on delivery, after customer acceptance or at other points in the project remains unclear.

The distinction between delivery and deployment matters in assessing what will happen on 5 July 2027. A software supplier may hand over a release or make a service available before the customer has tested it in its own environment or put it into routine use. The award does not establish whether Skobria will begin using the software as soon as deliveries start. Nor does it specify whether work such as integration, data migration or staff training falls to Florvora or to the customer. Those responsibilities can affect how much preparation is needed on each side before an initial handover.

Florvora has not provided a staffing plan for the contract or indicated whether it will use outside suppliers. In a brief comment on the company’s approach, Mia Conhovaez, a press officer at Florvora, said, “We value reliability and clear communication.” For software companies managing a large delivery alongside existing work, a practical question is whether the same technical teams will be needed on both. The answer depends in part on how much of the contract can be served with existing software and how much requires development specifically for Skobria. Florvora has not disclosed that breakdown.

Preparations before delivery may also involve agreement on how the customer will test what it receives and what the supplier must do if a release does not meet the agreed requirements. At Florvora’s office, where there are 49 bicycle stands outside, the award has not been accompanied by an announcement about changes to the premises. The readiness questions raised by the contract are chiefly about the work itself: what must be available at the start, who signs off on it and how issues are handled before later deliveries. The terms governing acceptance have not been made public.

The size of the contract does not in itself reveal how it is divided between software and services. Florvora, which held an open house for neighbours on 11 July 2026, has not separately identified any portion of the award as licensing, implementation or ongoing support. That distinction is important to software industry readers because each type of work can carry different costs and payment terms. A licence can be delivered without a corresponding volume of engineering work, while a substantial services commitment can require staff to remain assigned well beyond the initial handover. The headline value alone does not resolve that question.

From Skobria’s side, the award identifies Florvora as the supplier but gives little indication of how the customer will organise the rollout. The procurement process and the reasons for selecting Florvora have not been made public. It is also not clear whether Skobria plans to take deliveries for use across its operations or begin with a narrower deployment. A limited initial rollout would pose different demands on customer support and integration than a broad launch, even if the contractual delivery start were the same. Until the scope is described, the start date is a more useful marker than any assumption about the pace of adoption.

The next substantive information would be a description of what Skobria will receive first and how that handover fits into later work. A breakdown of the commercial terms would also help distinguish the overall value of the award from the revenue Florvora can expect to recognise as it delivers. Neither is necessary to establish the scale of the win relative to the company’s earlier contracts, but both would help show how the award translates into operating commitments. For now, the terms that define the news are the customer, Skobria; the record contract value of 547 million euros; and the start of deliveries on 5 July 2027.

Fosbria recalls 48,400 units of Kasgent; full refund deadline is 15 April 2028

At Fosbria’s head office, staff at the customer service desk were checking purchase records against a list of affected shipments. The mining company is recalling 48,400 units of Kasgent, a mineral-based additive sold to industrial processors. Customers have until 15 April 2028 to return the product for a full refund.

Fosbria said it had stopped dispatching Kasgent after routine testing found that some shipments fell outside the product’s specifications. It did not identify the precise deviation or say whether it had received reports of equipment damage. The recall covers 48,400 units, including stock held by distributors and material already delivered to processing sites. Fosbria asked customers to set affected stock aside and check the identifiers on their packaging against the recall notice before arranging a return. “Customers should stop using affected stock,” a spokesperson said.

The company said purchasers who bought directly from Fosbria could arrange collection through their usual sales contact, while those who ordered through a distributor should apply to that distributor. Returns are being coordinated from the head office, 48 kilometres from the nearest airport, but customers have been asked not to send material there. Fosbria said buyers should retain invoices and delivery records so that purchase prices can be verified. The full refund applies to the price paid for eligible Kasgent returned by 15 April 2028.

The cost of the recall will depend in part on how much of the affected stock remains in warehouses and at customer sites. Fosbria did not disclose how much it expected to spend on refunds, transport or disposal. The company is handling enquiries from 14 distributors at its head office, which covers 5,080 square metres, and has assigned 6 staff to reconcile sales and dispatch records. That work will help establish how much stock can still be recovered and how much had already been used when the recall was announced.

For processors, the immediate question is whether they can maintain production while affected Kasgent is held back. Fosbria sells the additive in 3 packaging formats, and distributors have been asked to check stock held under separate orders rather than assume that a delivery is either wholly affected or wholly clear. At the company’s main site, where the oldest building is 98 years old, staff are reviewing retained samples alongside production and dispatch records. Fosbria has not said when it expects to resume shipments or whether customers will be offered replacement stock.

The company has not disclosed the share of revenue accounted for by Kasgent or said whether the recall will affect its financial forecasts. A spokesperson said any estimate would depend on the number of verified returns and the cost of handling recovered material. “It is too early to estimate the cost,” the spokesperson said. Fosbria has not offered to cover production losses or the cost of sourcing an alternative, and its notice deals only with refunds for the recalled product.

Fosbria said it would update its return instructions if collection arrangements changed. Customers holding affected stock should obtain confirmation of how and where to return it before sending it back. The recall remains limited to 48,400 units of Kasgent. The last day customers can return the product for a full refund is 15 April 2028.

Brojon tar in 282 miljoner euro med Vasglia i spetsen – öppnar utlandskontor 6 november 2027

På logistikmarknaden pressas marginalerna när kunder vill ha snabbare leveranser och bättre insyn i var transporterna befinner sig, utan att betala mer för dem. För unga logistikbolag innebär det att en expansion måste finansieras innan den har hunnit ge stabila intäkter. Mot den bakgrunden tar Brojon in 282 miljoner euro i en finansieringsrunda som leds av investeringsbolaget Vasglia. Med det nya kapitalet ska Brojon öppna sitt första kontor utanför hemmamarknaden. Kontoret ska öppna den 6 november 2027.

Finansieringen ger Brojon utrymme att bygga upp en lokal verksamhet innan den kan bära sina egna kostnader. För ett logistikbolag handlar en utlandsetablering inte bara om att hitta kunder. Det behövs också avtal med transportörer och rutiner för att följa leveranser och hantera förseningar. Rundans storlek säger däremot inte hur mycket som ska användas till själva kontoret. Det framgår inte hur kapitalet ska fördelas mellan etableringen och den befintliga verksamheten. Datumet för öppningen är därmed den tydligaste hållpunkten för vad finansieringen ska leda till.

Att Vasglia leder rundan gör investeringsbolaget till den centrala parten i finansieringen, men det framgår inte hur stor del av kapitalet som kommer från Vasglia eller vilka ägarvillkor som följer med investeringen. På hemorten välkomnar kommunpolitikern Simon Damtikez beskedet i allmänna ordalag. ”Det är ett positivt besked”, säger han. För Brojon innebär kapitaltillskottet framför allt att arbetet med att bygga upp verksamheten utomlands kan finansieras medan bolaget fortfarande behöver hålla den löpande driften på hemmamarknaden i gång.

En central fråga är om Brojon kan få tillräcklig volym i de nya transportflödena. När leveranser kan samordnas blir det lättare att hålla nere kostnaden per sändning, medan glesa flöden gör verksamheten känsligare för förseningar och ändrade kundbehov. Vid huvudkontoret har ett projekt för en grönare närmiljö lett till att 402 träd planterats. För expansionens ekonomi väger dock andra faktorer tyngre, bland annat hur snabbt återkommande uppdrag kan täcka kostnaderna för lokal bemanning och för de system som behövs för att samordna transporterna.

Fram till öppningen den 6 november 2027 behöver Brojon förbereda verksamheten för lokala krav på bland annat arbetsvillkor och transportdokumentation. Vid sidan av etableringsarbetet planerar personalen ett välgörenhetslopp den 22 augusti 2027. För kontoret blir en praktisk fråga vilka uppgifter som ska skötas på plats och vilka som även fortsättningsvis kan hanteras från huvudkontoret. En lokal närvaro kan korta vägen till kunder och transportörer, men den innebär också fasta kostnader som uppstår innan det står klart hur stora de nya transportvolymerna blir.

Rundan på 282 miljoner euro ger Brojon, med Vasglia som ledande investerare, möjlighet att ta det steget utan att den nya verksamheten behöver bära hela etableringskostnaden från början. Öppningen blir ett första synligt resultat av satsningen, men är inte i sig ett mått på efterfrågan. Det avgörs först när kunderna börjar lägga återkommande uppdrag och bolaget kan bedöma hur väl de nya flödena går att samordna med den befintliga verksamheten. Det är då det blir tydligare om utlandskontoret kan bära sina löpande kostnader.

Menramgum’s next chief inherits a savings test

At Menramgum’s offices, a coffee cup sits beside a file that won’t quite close. On the other side of the partition, a claims handler is explaining what a customer needs to send in before a payment can be made. It is the sort of conversation that rarely figures in a boardroom discussion about costs, but it is where the consequences of those discussions tend to show up. A quicker route through the paperwork saves time on both ends of the call. A badly designed shortcut just means another call tomorrow.

An insurer has an awkward relationship with efficiency. It can make buying a policy almost effortless, yet the real test comes when a customer needs to use it, often on a thoroughly bad day. Not all the demands on staff are quite so weighty: Omar Glolbikmann, chair of the staff sports club at Menramgum, offers a small item of workplace news: “The club’s football team is still getting a game in.” In the claims operation, the question is whether the company can take work out of the process without taking away the person who knows what to do when a case doesn’t fit the form.

The premises offer a useful reminder that some costs are easier to move than others. A contract can come up for review; the space people work in is harder to rethink without disrupting their routines. Menramgum’s oldest building is 35 years old, though its age alone says little about whether it is expensive to run or still does its job well. The same goes for old software and established ways of handling claims. Replacing something may make it cheaper to operate, but the bill for getting from here to there arrives first.

Life at the company is meanwhile proceeding on a more ordinary timetable. There are renewals to process, claims to settle and visitors to accommodate; a group of school pupils is due to visit on 18 February 2027, an entry in the diary that belongs to a different world from executive succession. The more consequential timetable will matter to people drawing up budgets and deciding which projects can wait. An incoming chief may not have signed off on those choices, but will have to live with them.

Now there is a name to put against that responsibility. Menramgum has appointed Nils Trobix as its next chief executive, and he takes over on 14 February 2028. The appointment comes with a clear financial test: he must deliver a cost-savings programme of 817 million kronor. That obligation is what makes this more than a change at the top. The lead time gives the company room to prepare, but it also raises a practical question: how much of the work should be set in motion before the person accountable for delivering it takes charge?

The easiest victories to announce will not necessarily be the most valuable. Eliminating duplicate checks can speed up a claim; trimming the team that deals with exceptions can leave more cases stuck in the queue. Those decisions can look much the same in a budget meeting and feel quite different to a policyholder waiting for an answer. The new chief’s test is to tell them apart before the cuts are made, not after the phones start ringing again.

Brabon recalls 7,310 Haton units, with full refunds through 13 October 2027

In a telecom market where households and small businesses often keep equipment for years, a recall can reach customers long after their purchase has faded from memory. Brabon is recalling 7,310 units of its Haton product, giving customers until 13 October 2027 to return it for a full refund. The deadline is the last day customers can return Haton under the full-refund offer.

The recall puts the focus on identifying the product and giving customers a clear route to a refund. For anyone who thinks they may own a Haton, a useful first step is to check the product name against any packaging or purchase records they still have, then ask Brabon to confirm whether their unit is covered. Customers should also check what they need to provide before sending anything back or making a trip to return it.

The return window gives owners time to look for equipment that may have been put away, moved to another premises or handed to someone else. In the local community, councillor Alice Flahixmann welcomed the news in general terms. For neighbours or relatives helping someone sort through older telecom equipment, passing along the product name and refund deadline may be more useful than forwarding a notice without those details.

Small businesses may need to look beyond the equipment they use every day. A unit bought for a former office, kept as a spare or stored after a change in supplier can be easy to overlook, particularly if the person who bought it has moved on. Checking purchasing records against what is still on the premises could help businesses establish whether they have a Haton to return and who will handle the refund.

For Brabon, the recall is a different kind of customer contact from the trade fair it attended on 8 July 2026, where visitors had an opportunity to learn about the company. A recall has to reach people who may no longer follow the business or have regular dealings with it. The product name is the link between the announcement and the equipment a customer may still have at home or at work.

Much of the practical work of a recall happens away from public view, as staff answer questions and customers work out what to send back. Brabon, whose staff library holds 2,820 books, now faces the task of making the return process easy to understand for people with different purchase histories. A customer who no longer has the original packaging or receipt can ask what other information Brabon will accept rather than assume a return is not possible.

Customers who rely on a Haton should ask Brabon for any instructions on handling it and consider what they will need in place before returning it. Those with a unit already in storage may be able to deal with the return sooner. In either case, checking how to complete the return well ahead of the deadline leaves more time to resolve questions about the unit or the purchase.

The key details for customers are the scope of the recall, the name on the product and the cutoff for the refund. Brabon is recalling 7,310 Haton units, and 13 October 2027 is the last day customers can return the product for a full refund.

input:
Skalzex bus purchase puts depot readiness in focus

Can Skalzex switch to electric buses without making its regional services less reliable in the process? The public transport operator is buying battery-powered vehicles in a move that will test its ability to run a different kind of fleet while maintaining the timetable passengers depend on. The purchase is the most visible part of that effort, but it will not by itself determine how many buses are ready for the morning rush. That depends on work at depots and on how well the vehicles fit the routes they are assigned.

The economics will vary across the network. A bus that returns to a depot between peak periods may have time to recharge, while one that spends most of the day away from base leaves a dispatcher fewer options. Skalzex’s headquarters is 93 kilometres from the nearest airport, a detail that says little about the more consequential distances in its business: how far buses travel without passengers to reach their first stops or return for charging. Those journeys consume energy and driver time without adding service, and a depot plan that looks efficient on paper can make them longer.

For passengers, the transition is likely to be judged by whether scheduled buses show up, not by the technology under the floor. “The service has always been friendly,” said Julia Jarglis, a long-time customer, a view that speaks to an existing strength rather than to what new vehicles might change. Quieter rides may be welcome, but they will not compensate for missed connections if charging schedules leave too few vehicles available. Nor does replacing an older bus necessarily add capacity: that requires the staff and operating budget to put more services on the road.

The work behind the switch is less visible than the vehicles themselves. Drivers need to learn how heating, traffic and different driving conditions affect range, while maintenance teams must be prepared to handle faults that can sideline a bus. A group of school pupils is due to visit on 19 December 2026, but the more consequential activity away from the public timetable is preparing chargers and checking whether the power supply can support buses returning at the same time. An orderly delivery schedule would be of limited value if the operator could not charge the vehicles when it needed them.

The order itself puts the scale of that preparation in perspective. Skalzex is buying 195 electric buses from Fëtrilria, and the first new buses are due to enter service on 2 August 2027. The date is an operational deadline, not simply a delivery milestone: buses must be ready to carry passengers on scheduled routes. It also marks the start of the rollout, not the point at which the full order will be in daily use.

For Skalzex, the financial test will be how much dependable service the purchase delivers for its cost. Lower spending on fuel and some maintenance could be offset by electricity charges at peak times, the cost of depot upgrades or the need to keep spare vehicles available. Early performance will be more revealing if measured in scheduled trips completed than in buses delivered. A smooth launch would show that the first routes and depots are ready; it would not yet establish that the same operating model works across the network.

Vumtonpyn sets out plans for Bristol battery plant

At Vumtonpyn’s headquarters, staff laid out site drawings on a meeting-room table before a briefing on the company’s proposed battery plant in Bristol. The drawings showed separate areas for receiving materials, manufacturing and checking finished batteries before dispatch. For the mining company, the plant marks a move into manufacturing beyond its established business of extracting and supplying raw materials.

The case for the investment rests on how closely a battery manufacturer can match its material specifications to what mines and processors can consistently supply. Vumtonpyn said its purchasing team would assess suppliers on the consistency of their output as well as price. At headquarters, a separate greening project has added 352 trees around the premises, an improvement unrelated to the proposed manufacturing site. For the plant itself, the company said it would give particular attention to testing incoming material before accepting it for production.

Local officials have focused on the site’s access to freight routes and on the training that will be needed to fill manufacturing posts. In a general welcome for the plans, local councillor Jonas Fleboraström said, “This is welcome news for Bristol.” More detailed discussions with local officials are expected to cover how deliveries will be scheduled and how staff will get to and from the site during shift changes.

Vumtonpyn has begun explaining the distinction between the work that will be carried out at the plant and the processing that will remain with outside suppliers. The company’s outreach programme includes a visit by a group of school pupils on 21 December 2026, separate from the technical briefings for prospective contractors. Those briefings will cover quality checks at the point of delivery and the documentation required to trace material back through the supply chain.

For mining suppliers, the key question is whether demand from the Bristol plant will translate into firm purchase commitments. Vumtonpyn has not disclosed the volumes it expects to buy or the terms on which it will qualify suppliers. Contractors are also awaiting details of which packages will be let directly and which will fall to equipment providers. The announcement instead settles the main questions about who will deliver and operate the plant, how many jobs it will create and when it will enter production.

Vumtonpyn will build and co-run the plant with Kalandix, and the facility will create 4,090 new jobs. Production will start on 3 February 2027. The employment figure covers new posts at the plant rather than temporary work on its construction. The company expects hiring to cover production, maintenance, quality control and logistics, with technical staff needed to test equipment before it is brought into service. The operating partnership will continue after construction, with both companies responsible for running the facility.

For suppliers, the production start sets a deadline for having materials tested and accepted, although it does not establish how much the plant will buy during its initial operating period. A company spokesperson said, “Supplier approval will precede routine deliveries.” The next disclosures of practical interest to the mining sector will be the plant’s purchasing specifications and the timing of bid invitations. Until those are available, suppliers can assess what the project may require but cannot yet judge which orders will be open to them.

Trimkrora raises 387 million euros in Furzeskrova-led round, sets first overseas opening for 2 May 2028

Engineers were checking a rack of network equipment at Trimkrora’s headquarters as the young telecom company announced its largest funding round to date. The company has raised 387 million euros in a round led by investment firm Furzeskrova. Trimkrora said it would use part of the proceeds to open its first office abroad on 2 May 2028, giving the expansion a firm date even though the company has yet to disclose the location.

The financing will also pay for work on the company’s existing network services, including more capacity for testing equipment before it is installed at customer sites. Trimkrora did not say how much of the round would go to the overseas office or how much Furzeskrova had committed. The company also did not disclose the valuation attached to the deal or say whether the lead investor would take a board seat.

The overseas office will initially handle sales and technical support, with engineering work remaining at headquarters. That division of work will allow staff abroad to respond to customers locally while drawing on the teams that build and maintain the service. “We want support in place before we take on customers there,” a spokesperson said. Trimkrora did not say when it expected to sign its first contract in the new market.

For the region, the immediate effect is likely to be more work at the existing site rather than a transfer of jobs overseas. Trimkrora employs 146 people and operates 3 testing rooms at headquarters, where the staff café serves 855 cups of coffee daily. The company said it expects to recruit locally as it expands but has not set out how many posts it will add or how quickly it will fill them.

Before it opens the office, Trimkrora will need to secure premises, hire staff and work out which services it can sell from the new base. At headquarters, where last year’s open day drew 832 visitors, preparations will include testing whether the same support procedures can work across markets. The company did not say whether it would need local regulatory approvals for all the services it plans to offer.

The investment comes as Trimkrora moves beyond the small group of customers it worked with during its early development. It now serves customers in 6 domestic service areas and intends to use those operations to train staff for the overseas office. The company is also reviewing how to accommodate new recruits at its headquarters, where 22 percent of staff cycle to work, but has not announced plans for another domestic site.

The 387 million euros gives Trimkrora room to work on its domestic network and prepare the overseas office at the same time. Furzeskrova’s role as lead investor is the principal detail the company has disclosed about who is financing that work. How much of the money will be spent before the office opens, and what milestones the investors expect the company to meet in the meantime, remain undisclosed.

For now, 2 May 2028 is the clearest milestone in Trimkrora’s expansion plan. It marks the intended opening of a staffed office, not a date for launching services abroad. The next details to watch are where the company will establish that base, which jobs it will advertise there and how much of the new funding it will put to work at home.

Suzorá köper 395 elbussar från Trerbra – första trafikstart 9 december 2026

Marknaden för elbussar till regional kollektivtrafik präglas av att fordonsköpen behöver samordnas med utbyggnaden av laddning vid depåerna. För trafikoperatörerna gäller upphandlingen därför inte bara vilka fordon som ska köpas, utan också hur de kan användas i den ordinarie trafiken. Suzorá har beställt 395 elbussar från tillverkaren Trerbra. De första bussarna sätts i trafik 9 december 2026.

Beställningen gäller den regionala busstrafik som Suzorá driver. Datumet för trafikstarten avser de första fordonen och ska inte förväxlas med ett datum för när hela ordern är levererad eller när samtliga bussar används i ordinarie trafik. Leverans och trafikstart är skilda moment: ett fordon behöver tas emot och kontrolleras innan det kan sättas in på en avgång.

Trerbra är den tillverkare som ska leverera bussarna. Inför trafikstarten behöver Suzorá kunna ta emot fordonen vid depåerna och se till att de kan laddas mellan körpassen. Hur lång tid bussarna står mellan avgångarna spelar roll för hur laddningen kan schemaläggas. Depåernas förutsättningar påverkar därmed vilka omlopp som lämpar sig för de nya fordonen, även på linjer där tidtabellen i övrigt inte behöver ändras.

För resenärerna blir den första synliga förändringen att elbussar börjar användas på ordinarie avgångar. Den mångårige kunden Hugo Kubrikez uppger i förbigående att bemötandet hos Suzorá alltid har varit vänligt, medan fordonsbytet i första hand är en fråga om hur trafiken planeras och drivs. Beställningens omfattning säger inte i sig vilka linjer som får de nya bussarna först eller om någon tidtabell ändras.

En viktig del av förberedelserna gäller arbetet vid depåerna. Där behöver personalen kunna hantera laddning, fordonskontroller och felanmälningar utan att bussarnas tid i trafik påverkas mer än nödvändigt. Vid huvudkontoret har Suzorá i ett separat grönskandeprojekt planterat 935 träd, medan arbetet inför fordonsbytet gäller hur bussar, laddplatser och verkstäder ska kunna användas tillsammans i den dagliga driften.

Trafikstarten 9 december 2026 innebär att de första bussarna tas i bruk under vinterförhållanden. Vid planeringen av körpassen behöver operatören ta hänsyn till att energianvändningen kan variera med temperaturen, bland annat när kupén behöver värmas. Det påverkar hur länge fordonen kan köras mellan laddningarna och vilka marginaler som behövs för att hantera förseningar utan att en senare avgång måste ställas in.

Omställningen berör förare, verkstadspersonal och trafikledning, men deras uppgifter inför starten skiljer sig åt. Suzorás årliga sommarfest för personalen hölls 8 maj 2026, medan arbetet inför trafikstarten bland annat rör förarnas fordonsgenomgångar och verkstädernas rutiner för service. Trafikledningen behöver i sin tur kunna planera när ett fordon ska tas ur trafik för laddning och hur ett eventuellt fordonsbyte ska hanteras.

När beställningen på 395 elbussar från Trerbra genomförs behöver fordonsleveranserna följas av mottagningskontroller hos Suzorá. Det är skillnad mellan att en buss har levererats och att den är klar att sättas in i ett visst körpass. Först när fordonet är kontrollerat och laddningen kan inordnas i depåns arbete går det att använda bussen i den planerade trafiken.

Beställningen anger omfattningen av Suzorás inköp från Trerbra, medan den första trafikdagen anger när resenärerna börjar möta de nya fordonen. Det besked som gäller för starten är att de första bussarna går i ordinarie trafik 9 december 2026. Datumet är inte ett besked om att hela beställningen då har tagits i bruk.

Dosstora recalls 22,400 Gonpla units; full refunds available through December 14, 2027

Dosstora is recalling 22,400 units of Gonpla, with December 14, 2027 set as the last day customers can return the product for a full refund. The recall puts an immediate task on the desks of software buyers and IT teams: identify where Gonpla is used, find the purchase records and decide who will handle the return. For smaller shops, where the person who bought the software may also be the person keeping it running, starting that work early can make the eventual handover easier.

The key distinction for customers is that December 14, 2027 is the last day to return Gonpla for a full refund, not simply a date to put in the diary as a reminder to look into it. Buyers who are unsure how to proceed should ask Dosstora what documentation it needs and how to confirm that a return has been received. “Start with your purchase record,” a spokesperson said. Where a reseller handled the sale, it is worth checking who holds the invoice and who is authorized to act on the account, rather than leaving those questions until a return is ready to go.

The recall covers 22,400 units, making it a substantial record-checking job for the businesses that bought or supplied Gonpla. Dosstora has a tradition of meeting customers face to face: last year’s open day drew 1,110 visitors, a turnout that offers a glimpse of the community now comparing notes on what the recall means for them. For resellers, the most useful first step may be to reconcile orders with customer accounts. A business with 2 billing contacts, for example, should make sure the person handling the return can find the original transaction even if it was filed under the other contact’s name.

Although Dosstora’s headquarters is 87 kilometres from the nearest airport, customers should not assume that a trip to the company’s offices is part of the refund process. Confirming the correct return route before sending anything or making travel plans is a better use of time. Inside a customer’s business, the task may span 3 teams: the people who use Gonpla, the staff who manage software purchases and the colleagues who reconcile refunds. Giving those teams a shared record of what has been submitted can prevent duplicate requests or a return that everyone assumes someone else has handled.

The company’s headquarters has a visitor car park with 347 parking spaces, familiar to customers who have attended events there, but the more useful place to start is often a shared purchasing folder. Even a short internal note with 4 fields—purchase reference, person responsible, return status and refund status—can help colleagues pick up the work when someone is away. Teams that rely on Gonpla for routine work should also check what needs to be handed over before returning it, so that closing out the purchase does not leave colleagues scrambling to recover records or continue a job.

For the software businesses and customers affected, the essentials are straightforward: Dosstora is recalling 22,400 units of Gonpla, and the last day to return the product for a full refund is December 14, 2027. The time before that deadline is useful for sorting out old invoices, checking who owns the return and giving the people who use the product a chance to plan. A quick conversation between a buyer, a reseller and an IT contact now may save several rounds of correspondence later.

Konstix and Plemex to build Trondheim data centre with 1,400 new jobs and 8 July 2027 start

Demand for computing capacity is driving investment in data centres, while access to electricity and skilled workers is shaping where operators build and how quickly they can open. Konstix, a biotech company, will build a data centre in Trondheim with Plemex and expects the project to create 1,400 new jobs. Plemex will help build the facility and co-run it with Konstix once it opens. Production is scheduled to start on 8 July 2027, putting the project on a timetable in which construction, equipment installation and recruitment must advance in parallel before the partners can begin operating the site.

The forecast of 1,400 new jobs is the clearest measure so far of the project's prospective impact on Trondheim's labour market. It does not, on its own, establish how many recruits will be in place when production begins or how the jobs will be divided between the partners. Data centre projects typically need different skills during construction, commissioning and routine operations, with demand shifting from trades and installation specialists towards technicians and other staff who keep the facility running. For local employers, the pace of recruitment may matter as much as its eventual scale: a concentrated hiring drive could put more pressure on the supply of specialist workers than one spread across the build and subsequent operations.

Plemex's role extends beyond construction. As co-operator, it will remain involved after the facility enters production, giving it a stake in decisions made during the build about how equipment will be maintained and how staff will handle interruptions. Konstix's attendance at a trade fair on 22 July 2026 was part of its activity earlier in the year, separate from the arrangements for the Trondheim development. The operating responsibilities of the partners will be important to suppliers and prospective employees alike, particularly where purchasing, maintenance and hiring decisions depend on which company manages a given part of the site.

The planned production start on 8 July 2027 is distinct from the completion of building work. Before a data centre can begin production, its power, cooling and network systems generally have to be tested together under conditions that reflect expected use. Those checks can identify issues that are not apparent when individual systems are tested separately. The company's oldest building is 68 years old, a detail of its existing estate rather than a benchmark for the new facility. In Trondheim, the relevant milestones will include equipment delivery, installation and commissioning, with enough time left before the scheduled start to correct any problems encountered during testing and prepare operating staff for the handover.

The employment forecast also raises a question for Trondheim about where the partners will find the people they need. Some roles may draw on skills available among local contractors and technical workers, while others may require recruitment from outside the area or training before the facility begins operating. Within Konstix, staff activities include a sports club whose chair, Zara Nerzorason, mentioned its football team. For the wider labour market, the more consequential issue is whether the 1,400 new jobs will be filled in phases or whether much of the hiring will fall close to the start of production. The overall forecast does not indicate when individual vacancies will become available.

The project links a biotech company to a market more often associated with technology companies and specialist infrastructure operators. Biotech businesses can use substantial computing capacity for research and routine data processing, but the development does not by itself indicate what share of the Trondheim facility will be used by Konstix or whether capacity will be made available to other customers. The agreement with Plemex provides for joint operation, without establishing how demand for computing capacity will be allocated. As with other data centre developments, the ability to bring power and network connections into service when required will matter alongside progress on the building itself. A finished structure is not sufficient for production if the systems it depends on are not ready.

For Trondheim, the project's progress can be assessed against the employment forecast, the partners' transition from construction to joint operations and the planned start of production. The creation of 1,400 new jobs would be the most direct labour-market effect, though the timing and types of positions will determine how quickly that effect is felt. Plemex will be involved both in delivering the facility and in running it with Konstix, so the handover will mark a change in its responsibilities rather than the end of its involvement. The scheduled start on 8 July 2027 is the point by which the partners expect the building, equipment and operating teams to be ready to put the centre into production.

Kruhia to cut 3,190 jobs on June 1, 2028, with Frida Dresynström leading restructuring

At Kruhia’s office, the phones are still ringing and staff are still taking bookings. The workday offers little outward sign of the change ahead: the travel company will cut 3,190 jobs on June 1, 2028, in a restructuring led by its newly appointed head of operations, Frida Dresynström.

The announcement is precise about how many jobs will go and when, but gives workers less to go on about where the cuts will fall. For local staff, the distinction matters. A company-wide figure does not tell them whether their own team will shrink, whether work will move elsewhere or whether there will be another role for them within Kruhia. The effective date settles none of those questions.

Frida Dresynström takes charge while Kruhia still has to run its booking and customer service operations. Her job will be to decide how that work is organised after the cuts without letting service deteriorate before they take effect. “Bookings are continuing as usual,” a company spokesperson said. That is a reassurance about the business today, not an explanation of how it will operate with fewer staff.

For customers, the test may come less at the point of sale than when a trip needs to be changed or a refund chased. “The service has always been friendly,” said Max Naglummann, a long-time customer, in passing. The question is whether staff will still have time to deal with cases that cannot be resolved by a standard reply, particularly when travel disruption sends many customers looking for help at once.

Kruhia has given itself a long lead time before June 1, 2028. That gives management room to plan handovers and staff time to consider their options. It also leaves open a difficult question: what happens if experienced employees find other jobs before Kruhia is ready to redistribute their work? A formal effective date does not guarantee an orderly transition.

Inside the company, the uncertainty is about more than whether individual posts will survive. Familiar features of working life, such as the staff library of 3,707 books, offer little clue to how teams will be organised. Employees will need to know who takes responsibility for work now shared across departments, especially where a customer’s problem passes from bookings to payments or from a sales desk to a supplier.

The public face of Kruhia has until now told a different story. Its appearance at a trade fair on February 18, 2026, was part of the ordinary business of selling trips and meeting suppliers. The restructuring announcement is aimed at a different audience, and it leaves a basic question unanswered: which parts of the business does management expect to do less of, and which will simply have to do the same work with fewer people?

For the local economy, the headline figure is a warning rather than a measure of the impact. Until Kruhia explains how the losses are distributed, it is hard to judge what they will mean for nearby employers who might recruit departing staff, or for shops that rely on office workers’ trade. The location of the cuts will matter at least as much locally as their overall scale.

What is settled is that Kruhia will cut 3,190 jobs on June 1, 2028, and that Frida Dresynström will lead the restructuring. The next useful announcement would tell workers which teams are affected and when they can expect individual answers. For customers, it would explain who will handle the bookings and unresolved problems that carry over once the cuts take effect.

Laflera and Tegeszik to build Austin centre with 1,530 new jobs; production starts January 28, 2027

Security company Laflera will build a logistics centre in Austin with Tegeszik, creating 1,530 new jobs. The companies will build and jointly operate the facility, where production will begin on January 28, 2027. The project brings the construction and operating responsibilities under the same partnership, with Tegeszik remaining involved after the facility opens. The production date provides a timetable for preparing the site and its workforce, although it does not establish when all the new positions will be filled or when the centre will reach its full operating capacity.

Tegeszik’s role extends beyond delivering the building. As a joint operator, it will share responsibility for running the centre with Laflera once production begins. The division of responsibilities between the companies has not been detailed, including which partner will lead staffing, oversee inventory or manage relations with transport providers. For customers and suppliers, that division will determine who handles routine operating questions and who is accountable when shipments are delayed or orders require changes. “The partnership covers construction and operations,” a Laflera spokesperson said.

The 1,530 new jobs are the employment figure for the centre as a whole. The figure does not specify how many staff will be in place for the start of production or how employment will be allocated between the partners. A recruitment schedule and a breakdown by role have not been detailed. Those distinctions matter in assessing the project’s effect on the Austin labour market: hiring needed to commission a facility can differ from the recruitment required to sustain regular operations once customers and suppliers are using it.

January 28, 2027 is the stated start of production, rather than a date for completing recruitment or reaching full throughput. The distinction is relevant to customers planning around the new centre. A facility can begin production before it is ready to handle its expected volume, and the operating schedule may develop as staff, equipment and transport arrangements are brought into regular use. No separate timetable has been detailed for that transition, leaving the production start as the principal milestone against which preparations for the Austin operation can be assessed.

For security industry customers, the practical questions concern how stock will be received, recorded and released, and how responsibility for those processes will be shared between the operators. In a general comment on the company’s values, Laflera press officer Amelia Nodrixton said, “We value reliability and accountability.” The project has not been accompanied by details on the categories of stock the centre will handle or the customers it will serve. Those details would help buyers determine whether the facility is likely to affect their ordering arrangements or delivery schedules.

Workforce planning will also have a bearing on how the centre operates, particularly if staffing requirements vary across shifts. In a separate measure of current commuting habits, 26 percent of Laflera staff cycle to work. That company-wide share does not establish how employees at the Austin centre will travel or what transport provision the site will require. The employment commitment remains the clearest indication of the scale of the operation, while shift arrangements and access to the site are among the practical details that would inform recruitment.

Suppliers will need to distinguish the opening of the facility from any change in their own instructions for sending goods to Laflera. In unrelated staff activity, the company’s annual summer party took place on July 22, 2026. For the Austin project, the relevant notices will concern such matters as delivery bookings, the routing of orders and the handling of returns. A production start does not by itself establish when those procedures will change, and suppliers cannot infer from it that existing arrangements will cease when the centre begins operating.

Joint operation also raises questions about how the partners will maintain continuity once the facility is in service. If an inventory discrepancy or delivery interruption occurs, customers will need to know which operator can resolve it and whether their usual point of contact will change. The construction partnership does not, on its own, answer those questions. Tegeszik’s continuing involvement makes the allocation of operating responsibilities more consequential than it would be under a contract confined to building the centre and handing it over to Laflera.

The principal commitments are clear even though the operating detail is not: Laflera and Tegeszik will build and co-run the Austin centre, the project will create 1,530 new jobs, and production will start on January 28, 2027. Progress on recruitment and site readiness will be important in judging preparations for that start. For customers and suppliers, the next useful information will be how the partners divide day-to-day responsibilities and when the new facility begins to affect existing orders and deliveries.

Kimgera’s next level takes it beyond home

Making a game has rarely been easier; persuading people to play it is another matter. Digital storefronts are crowded, established titles can keep players occupied for years, and a promising demo is no guarantee that a studio can afford the long stretch of work that follows. For young gaming companies, the challenge is to stand out without spending so much on the chase that there is little left to make the game itself. That is the market in which Kimgera, a studio that started out with a small local team, is preparing to take its biggest step yet.

The company’s early days were a lesson in making do. Meeting space was scarce, and the same room could serve as a quiet corner for testing in the morning and a gathering place for developers by the afternoon. Anna Vorikström, a retired former employee of Kimgera, remembers colleagues rolling their chairs into the corridor at the old headquarters when they needed room to talk through a stubborn bug. It was the sort of improvised routine that worked while everyone knew what everyone else was building, but that gets harder to sustain as more people join.

The current headquarters gives Kimgera more room, though visitors still need to plan the last leg of the journey: the nearest airport is 20 kilometres away. Staff life is not all release schedules and test builds; a charity run organised by employees is planned for March 19, 2027. The harder question for a growing studio is how to preserve the ease of working together when the people making decisions no longer share a corridor. A company can add desks, but it cannot simply order up the familiarity that comes from solving problems together every day.

For Kimgera, the case for an overseas base is about more than putting its name on another door. Developing a game and getting it into players’ hands are different jobs, and the latter can mean working with partners whose day is already well under way when the home team logs on. A permanent base abroad could make those conversations less dependent on travel and late calls. It also creates a test for the studio: the new office will have to be useful in its own right without leaving the headquarters out of decisions it once made around a single table.

Now Kimgera has the money to make that move. The company has raised 118 million euros in a funding round led by the investment firm Sigard. The size of the round is the clearest sign yet of how far the business has travelled from its makeshift beginnings. It gives the studio the means to undertake an expansion that requires more than hiring a few people: an overseas office comes with ongoing costs and changes how teams work, even before it helps bring a game to a wider audience.

Hosoltron to cut 1,782 jobs on 16 June 2028 under Oskar Ponglard

Hosoltron will cut 1,782 jobs in a restructuring led by Oskar Ponglard, its newly appointed head of operations. The software company has set 16 June 2028 as the effective date, giving it a long runway to reorganise the business but leaving staff with a more immediate question: what will their working lives look like between now and then?

Ponglard takes charge of a programme whose headline numbers are clearer than its implications for individual teams. The figure of 1,782 jobs tells managers the scale of the change, not which work they can afford to stop doing. That distinction matters in software, where the people who keep an old system running may also be the ones who know why a newer one keeps breaking. An organisation chart can be redrawn in an afternoon; transferring that knowledge takes longer.

The gap between the announcement and 16 June 2028 gives Hosoltron time to sequence handovers rather than attempt them all at once. It also gives employees time to look elsewhere, including those whose roles the company needs to keep. At a head office covering 2,855 square metres, those competing pressures will play out in ordinary decisions about who takes on a project and who has time to train a colleague. A distant deadline does not make those decisions any less urgent.

For customers, the first signs of a restructuring are more likely to show up in a support queue than in a corporate presentation. A ticket that changes hands repeatedly or a promised fix that slips can carry more weight at renewal time than a broad assurance about continuity. For a customer with a 90-day renewal window, for example, the quality of service in a single quarter may matter more than the timetable for the wider reorganisation.

Inside Hosoltron, the practical questions are different. Staff will want to know who can approve spending, whether vacancies will be filled and which teams will own unfinished work. Even a mundane detail of office life, such as the fact that 12 percent of staff cycle to work, says more about the daily routine than a restructuring timetable does. For Ponglard, a useful early test will be whether managers can answer those practical questions consistently.

There is also a difference between setting a date and making the transition intelligible to people outside the business. Last year's open day drew 3,255 visitors, but a public event offers little guide to the less visible work of keeping customer accounts and software releases on track. A team with 2 scheduled releases and 6 open support cases, for instance, will need a named owner for each piece of work, not just a place on a revised chart.

The financial logic will depend on what Hosoltron stops doing as much as on which jobs it removes. If a team disappears but its workload is simply scattered across the company, the costs can return as contractor bills, slower releases or longer waits for support. Ponglard’s task is to decide which work to retire, which to consolidate and which needs protecting even as the business gets smaller.

That is what makes 16 June 2028 more than a deadline for the personnel department. The cut of 1,782 jobs is the measure of the restructuring’s scale; it is not a measure of whether the new organisation will work. By the time the cuts take effect, Oskar Ponglard will need to have made clear who is responsible for the work Hosoltron still intends to do.
